item.title: Iran says it is 'fully prepared' to counter widened US economic sanctions
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0qxew81y83o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Iran says it is 'fully prepared' to counter widened US economic sanctions - Published Iran has said it is confident it can counter widened US sanctions after Washington announced what it described as an "economic D-Day" against the country to try to isolate it from the global economy. Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran was "fully prepared" for the sanctions, which he said would lead to "another defeat" for the US. Announcing a raft of new measures, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated, and that banks and businesses dealing with Iran would share its isolation if they refused to cut ties. The latest moves follow U-turns and extended deadlines from the White House in its efforts to end the conflict. Bessent described the new measures as "the single greatest financial offensive ever" against Iran, which would "tighten the noose and block every potential source of revenue". Iran's largest trading partners include China, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates – which announced last week it was halting all trade and financial transactions with Tehran. But hours after the US announcement, Iran said it was confident its trading partners would continue to do business. Madanizadeh said neither China nor Russia had "accepted" the US measures, and predicted other countries would resist them. "The government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," he told state television, adding that Tehran had been "waiting for these plans for a long time". "We also have our own tools and know how to play the game," he said. The Chinese Foreign Ministry said sanctions and pressure tactics did not help and Beijing would do what was necessary to protect China's interests. The war has led to hikes in global oil prices, and in response to the latest threat Iran warned it would shut down all oil exports from the region if the war continued. The Iranian regime has also issued a fresh warning to ships not to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without permission, according to Reuters. One fifth of the world's oil and gas usually passes through the strait - a narrow waterway south of Iran. But the flow has been effectively blocked by the country since the conflict began at the end of February, leading to higher oil prices globally. At a press conference earlier on Monday outlining what has been called "Operation Economic Outcast", Bessent said the US was launching an "economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe". "Iran now faces a very clear choice with only two paths before them: complete global isolation... or a path back to normalcy with an opportunity to rejoin the global economy," he said. The treasury secretary claimed America was "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it". Bessent said the Treasury had mapped networks, facilitators and financial channels used by Iran to evade sanctions to trade oil. The department said it had issued determinations against five sectors: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. The Treasury has also imposed sanctions on almost 60 entities, individuals and vessels. In a warning to governments and entities assisting or trading with Iran, he said they could not "claim they are blind to enabling this activity". He declined to highlight specific countries, but said Trump would be phoning world leaders "with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime". While he said it was important to give people time to understand the new sanctions, he added: "They should know that we will move very quickly and that we are serious." 'Damp squib' David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, cast doubt on the effectiveness of the sanctions announcement. "With the renewed US naval blockade already strangling Iran's oil exports, the direct impact of 'economic D-Day' on Iran's energy revenues will be somewhat of a damp squib," he said. "We suspect that the new package will have only a limited direct impact on Iranian energy flows in the short term." He said that was partly due to the fact roughly 90% of Iran's oil goes to China, a country "which has not recognised US sanctions in the past and is unlikely to be cowed this time either". Over the course of the conflict so far, previous threats have included Trump saying in April that "a whole civilisation will die tonight" unless Iran agreed a deal to end the war and unblock the Strait of Hormuz. The US eventually climbed down from that position after mediator Pakistan intervened and called for more diplomacy. The economic impact of the Iran war is being felt in the US and across the world. Higher oil prices have fuelled concerns over the cost of living, with petrol and diesel prices much higher than they were a year ago. In the US, gasoline prices have surpassed $4 a gallon and affordability is among the top concerns of American voters ahead of the mid-term elections in November. On Monday, a barrel of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, was $92. Last week, Bessent announced the US government would intervene in the bond markets and buy back more government debt in a bid to boost demand for bonds and lower borrowing rates. But the impact of the announcement was short-lived, with long-term borrowing costs bouncing back up a day later. - Iran nuclear deal: What it all means - Published23 November 2021 - How much could Trump's 'economic D-Day' hurt Iran? - Published4 days ago The Iranian regime already faces tough economic sanctions from the US. Former US President Barack Obama and several US allies had agreed a deal with the country in 2015 which lifted many sanctions in return for Iran agreeing to limit its nuclear programme. However, Trump pulled out of that deal in 2018, calling it "defective at its core", and reimposed all US sanctions on Iran. During Joe Biden's term as US president, he made some attempts to reinstate the Obama-era deal, but this did not happen. In April this year, the Trump administration launched a wave of sanctions on foreign banks and firms doing business with Tehran after it became clear its military operations had not caused Iran's regime to surrender.

item.title: Lockerbie bombing trial postponed days before it was due to start
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq63rmj1zl1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Lockerbie bombing trial postponed days before it was due to start - Published The trial of a Libyan man over the Lockerbie bombing has been postponed for a third time, after new evidence on the 37-year-old case came to light three days ago. Jury selection was due to get under way in Washington DC on Wednesday but the BBC understands a new start date has been set for January next year. Lawyers acting for Abu Agila Mohammad Kheir Al-Marimi said "newly discovered evidence" previously unknown to the defence and prosecutors from the US government emerged on Friday 21 August. Al-Marimi has denied building the bomb that destroyed Pan Am Flight 103 on December 21, 1988, killing 270 people. His lawyers told the court: "Constitutional and ethical obligations require the defence to investigate this development." They said they met Al-Marimi on Sunday and he agreed that they should ask for the postponement. The trial judge, Dabney Friedrich, has agreed that the start date should be set aside, underlining the potential importance of the new evidence. She would have been extremely reluctant to allow an 11th hour postponement after months of preparation and marathon pre-trial legal battles. For the relatives of those who died and Al-Marimi himself, this latest delay means a verdict might not come until next spring. It is yet another stunning development in a saga that has witnessed countless twists and turns over nearly four decades. Pan Am 103 was flying from Heathrow to New York when the bomb exploded in its forward hold, breaking the plane apart at 31,000 feet. All 259 passengers and crew on board were killed. Another 11 people died in Lockerbie when the wreckage fell on their homes. Of the victims, 190 were American and 43 from the UK. Nearly four decades later, the bombing remains the worst terror attack and mass murder in British history. 'Disappointing for the families' Al-Marimi has been in US custody since 2022 and was originally due to stand trial in May 2025. That date was set aside following a joint request from the prosecution and defence, who cited the complexity of the case and Al-Marimi's ill health. The trial was pencilled in for April this year but was called off again, after the defence asked for more time to prepare. The Lockerbie bombing has been the subject of a joint Scottish-US investigation since December 1988. Prosecutors from the Crown Office and detectives from Police Scotland were due to travel to Washington to attend the case, and Scottish witnesses were expected to be among the first to give evidence at the trial. Laura Buchan, head of the Lockerbie investigation team at the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service said: "I recognise that this adjournment will be disappointing for the families and for those who have followed this case over many years. "As the matter remains before the court, it would not be appropriate to comment on the reasons for the adjournment. Although these proceedings are being led by the United States authorities, Scottish prosecutors and police officers remain fully committed to supporting the pursuit of justice." A grandfather in his 70s, Al-Marimi has been accused of carrying out the attack along with two Libyans who faced a Scottish court in May 2000. Three judges heard the case at Camp Zeist, a former US air force base in the Netherlands. After eight months, they ruled the atrocity was an act of state sponsored terrorism carried out by members of the Libyan intelligence service. The judges convicted one of the Libyans, Abdulbasset Al-Megrahi, of mass murder and jailed him for life. He died from cancer in 2012, after being freed on compassionate grounds by the Scottish government. The Scottish Criminal Cases Review Conviction twice referred Megrahi's case to the appeal court but the conviction was upheld. The second Libyan, Al Amin Khalifah Fhimah was acquitted and returned home to a hero's welcome in Tripoli. The US government says Al-Marimi admitted bombing the plane along with Megrahi and Fhimah when he was questioned in a Libyan detention facility in 2012. The alleged confession was handed to Scottish investigators in 2017 and is now central to the prosecution case. Al-Marimi has claimed the confession is false and was made under duress, but judge Friedrich ruled it can be admitted as evidence at the trial. - Lockerbie bombing accused says he was forced into false confession - Published18 September 2025 Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. item.title: UK drone factories may face attacks from 'unknown sources', says Kremlin adviser
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg598m3meeyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
UK drone factories may face attacks from 'unknown sources', says Kremlin adviser - Published Andrei Fedorov, an adviser to the Kremlin, says there might be a "semi-military" response against UK drone factories by "unknown sources" over the sharing of blueprints for British-made cruise missile components. His comments on BBC Newsnight come as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he plans to travel to the US next month with European leaders to lobby US President Trump on Ukraine's defence needs. He said that while the details were not "fully confirmed", it is "likely" he will go. The trip would be his first to the US since becoming prime minister in July. "Leaving today, I'm quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks," he said following his official visit to Ukraine on Monday, during which he promised to continue pressuring Russia. The UK has also agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile. The blueprints will allow Ukraine to produce the long-range weapon domestically. Fedorov, who is Russia's former deputy foreign minister, said Putin was facing "serious" pressure "to undertake certain measures against UK". Asked on BBC Newsnight where the pressure was coming from, Fedorov responded, "public opinion polls, it's coming from journalists, from mass media". Asked what a "semi-military" response might look like, Fedorov said "it could take the form of something might happen with enterprises, with factories which are producing drones for Ukraine." "They could be attacked not by Russia, but by from unknown sources," he said. The comments are in line with those made by Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Monday, when he criticised the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints. Peskov said it prevented "even the slightest progress" towards achieving peace. He told reporters on Monday that the Russian military was already gathering data to locate any missile production sites to destroy them. "Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," he added. In response, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?" Burnham's visit to Ukraine was his first official international visit. He met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv and chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer. Burnham has been reaffirming the UK's support for Ukraine in the wake of escalating Russian strikes in recent weeks - including one last week on a shopping centre that killed at least 16 people. Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriot interceptor missiles, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles, but stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks. Zelensky has said he is hoping to secure 300 patriot missiles ahead of winter, when Russia is likely to increase its attacks on energy infrastructure, as it has done in past years. In the interview with Bloomberg, Burnham said that he felt "really confident" that the issue was "fixable". But he pointed out that it wasn't only the US who could supply Ukraine with Patriots. "There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with," he said. "It's probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation." In July this year, three weeks after offering Ukraine the right to produce Patriots itself, Trump backtracked, saying, "We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away, that kind of technology." "These weapons are incredible. We have to be very careful about letting somebody build them," Trump told a cabinet meeting. In a joint statement after the meeting in Ukraine, Burnham and co-chairs French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the group would aim to strength Kyiv's air defences "as a matter or urgent priority". They also condemned Moscow's "systemic and escalating strikes against Ukraine's cities, critical infrastructure and civilians" and pledged to "constrain Russia's war chest through sanctions and actions against the "shadow fleet". In a statement ahead of the visit, Burnham said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes. "I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security." He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace." Related topics - Published4 hours ago - Published17 hours ago

item.title: US removes Syria from list of state sponsors of terrorism
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c33knmyl0y5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US removes Syria from list of state sponsors of terrorism - Published The US has removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism after 47 years, lifting what it said was the "final major barriers" for private sector investment in the country and its reintegration into the global economy. US Secretary Of State Marco Rubio said the move was in recognition of the Syrian government's positive actions to fully distance itself from acts of international terrorism. The Trump administration has embraced Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former militant who once had an American bounty on his head as the leader of an al-Qaeda off-shoot. His Islamist group, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), was also removed from the US list of global terrorist organisations. HTS, formerly known as al-Nusra Front, was al-Qaeda's affiliate in Syria until Sharaa severed ties with the jihadist network in 2016. In late 2024, HTS led the rebel offensive that overthrew former president Bashar al-Assad and it dominates Sharaa's transitional administration. The US hopes to bring Syria into its orbit rather than that of Russia or China. But the risks remain significant, with Syria still far from secure and lacking representative government. It is also at the centre of growing tensions between its neighbours Israel and Turkey. Rubio said Monday's move, which had been initially flagged in July, would give the Syrians "a path to prosperity". US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "Today's action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability." Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani greeted the news as a "historic step", according to state-run news agency SANA. "We will continue working to remove the effects of isolation and create an environment based on transparency, mutual interests and respect," he said. Last year, the US also revoked the designation of HTS as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation and removed Sharaa from its list of Specially Designated Global Terrorists. Syria's removal from the US list of state sponsors of terrorism - where it had been since 1979 - leaves just three remaining: Cuba, North Korea and Iran. The listing carries financial sanctions, restrictions on US foreign aid and defence exports and sales and can also penalise people and other countries that trade with the sanctioned state. item.title: French tourist dies in Death Valley after car gets stuck in mud
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyl81jlzr2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
French tourist dies in Death Valley after car gets stuck in mud - Published A French tourist has died in California's Death Valley after becoming stranded on the side of the road during 46.6C (116F) heat. Police found 68-year-old Pierre Michel Formosa recently following a brief search, with the National Park service saying he died while trying to seek help in the blistering heat when his car got stuck in mud. "This is a heartbreaking reminder of how quickly conditions here can turn dangerous," Death Valley National Park Superintendent Mike Reynolds said in a statement. Soaring temperatures across the United States have caused millions of people to sweat through record heatwaves, leading to dozens of heat-related deaths. Formosa was driving through Death Valley with his French travelling companion last Monday when their vehicle became stuck in mud on West Side Road. The pair sought help by walking across the salt flats, before severe heat prevented the 68-year-old from continuing after 1.3 miles, according to the Death Valley National Park. The travelling companion managed to hail down a nearby driver, before rangers and police found Formosa later that afternoon where he was pronounced dead. "Death Valley is an extraordinary place, but its heat, distances, and remoteness can be dangerous, regardless of experience," Reynolds said. "We're grateful to everyone who took part in the search, and our thoughts are with his loved ones." Coroners would determine the cause and manner of his death, the national park said. An extreme heat warning is currently in effect across Death Valley, which brands itself as the "hottest place on Earth", according to its official website, having recorded a global high of 57C (134F) in 1913. Forecasters at the National Weather Service expected Southern California would experience its "hottest week of summer so far", the bureau said in a recent statement. Record heatwaves have endangered tourists visiting US landmarks throughout the summer. At least four hikers died in June while trekking through the Grand Canyon, state authorities reported in Arizona.

item.title: Kit Harington joins HBO's Harry Potter series as Gilderoy Lockhart
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c783lnz12vlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Kit Harington joins HBO's Harry Potter series as Gilderoy Lockhart - Published Kit Harington has been tapped to join the highly anticipated Harry Potter TV series as the wizarding world's celebrity-turned-Hogwarts instructor Gilderoy Lockhart, HBO confirmed to the BBC. Harington is replacing actor Nicholas Hoult who could not film season two of the series due to a scheduling conflict. Best known for playing Jon Snow for eight seasons in the award-winning series Game of Thrones, Harington also appears in the BBC and HBO financial drama Industry. The casting marks the English actor's third collaboration with the American network and streamer. Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone is due to premiere on Christmas this year on HBO Max. Season two will adapt the second book in the series by JK Rowling, The Chamber of Secrets, which chronicle's Potter's second year at the magical school. "Before we begin year two at Hogwarts, there has been a slight change due to schedule: Kit Harington will be stepping into the role of Gilderoy Lockhart," a story post reads on the official Harry Potter Instagram account. The new series adaptation of the best-selling books stars newcomer Dominic McLaughlin as the boy wizard, Alastair Stout as his best friend Ron Weasley and Arabella Stanton as the young witch Hermione Granger. Oscar-nominated actor Jon Lithgow has been cast as Hogwarts headmaster Albus Dumbledore and Nick Frost as gamekeeper Rubeus Hagrid. Emmy-award winning Harington, a lifelong fan of the books, already has some familiarity with his new role: The actor voiced Lockhart in Audible's star-studded Harry Potter: The Full-Cast Audio Editions last year. The show could reunite him with director and producer Mark Mylod, who worked on Game of Thrones and is directing some Harry Potter episodes. Mylod is an executive producer on the new series along with author JK Rowling. Lockhart was portrayed in the Warner Bros Harry Potter films by Kenneth Branagh, and is a key character in Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets, the second book in Rowling's best-selling franchise. The vain wizard who authored several books on his purported encounters with dark creatures serves as Hogwarts' latest professor for the defence against the dark arts and fancies himself a mentor to Harry in his second year. Hoult, known for his roles in X-Men, Superman and Mad Max: Fury Road, was announced for the role earlier this month. But HBO reportedly had to let the Superman actor out of his deal due to his commitments to projects that conflicted with a change in the series' production schedule, according to Deadline, which first reported Harington's casting. HBO confirmed the reporting to the BBC. Representatives for Harington and Hoult did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The HBO series is expected to take 10 years to complete, as producers plan multiple seasons covering each of Rowling's seven books, which the eight blockbuster films were originally based on. - Published26 February 2025 - Published25 March

Local authorities say about 2,800 households were still without electricity on Monday evening, while several roads were blocked. item.title: US-Canada trade war escalates as Trump threatens tariff hike on vehicles
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c93vpd60654o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US-Canada trade war escalates as Trump threatens tariff hike on vehicles - Published President Donald Trump has threatened to hike US tariffs on automobiles originating in Canada, as the trade war between the two neighbours continues to heat up. Trump said on Monday that he will increase tariffs on Canadian cars and trucks, as well as auto parts, from 25% to 50% as of 1 January. It comes after US-Canada trade talks collapsed late last week, with each side accusing the other of making unreasonable last-minute demands. Late on Monday, Canada officials announced a news conference on Tuesday where they would outline how the country would respond to the trade war and work to "protect and support Canadian workers and businesses during these challenging times". The news conference at 11:00 ET (16:00 BST) will include government leaders in business, finance and economic development. Earlier in the day, Prime Minister Mark Carney called Trump's latest levy threat unsurprising and accused the president of wanting to destroy Canada's auto industry. He added that Canada is ready to resume talks only if the US comes with the "right attitude". The war of words followed several US and Canadian officials saying that talks were suspended with no set date to resume. Canada walked away from trade negotiations late on Friday night, moments before a US-imposed deadline that would add a 50% levy on nearly $20bn (C$28bn; £14bn) of Canadian imports. The collapse in talks marked a significant change in tone from earlier in the week, when both sides appeared optimistic that a new US-Canada trade deal could be reached. Canadian officials have said the US introduced last-minute demands that were "unacceptable", including a clause limiting which countries Canada could sign trade deals with. US officials, meanwhile, said it was Canada that introduced last-minute changes. "They wanted more," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in an interview with CNBC on Monday. The breakdown led to growing tensions as both sides publicly dug in their heels. On Monday, Trump's tariff threats to Canada's auto industry followed Carney declaring the country would counter his levies with reciprocal tariffs on US goods "dollar for dollar". Carney said he was focused on supporting Canadian businesses impacted by new 50% US tariffs after the Friday deadline expired, as well as building infrastructure to diversify Canada's trade, which historically has relied heavily on the US. Carney announced funding of C$11bn ($7.95bn; £5.83bn) to build six icebreakers at a Quebec shipyard for the Canadian Coast Guard that will replace its medium and heavy ageing fleet. The icebreakers will be used to open winter shipping routes through Canada's northern and Atlantic waters. Meanwhile, Ontario's outspoken premier, Doug Ford, whose province is home to Canada's auto manufacturing industry, responded to Trump's tariffs and threats by telling the US president to "kiss my ass". Ford also suggested that Canada should charge the US extra for its oil and gas, as well as electricity and critical minerals, adding that he will be speaking to Carney on ways to "fight back". His comments appeared to catch the attention of Trump, who in a Truth Social post accused Ford of "bluster" and wrote: "Someone should get these clowns to 'fall in line' or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!". Canada accounts for 60% of total US crude oil imports and close to 100% of US natural gas exports, according to Canadian government data. Businesses on both sides have warned that they stand to be hurt by the new wave of US tariffs on Canada, as well as the retaliatory tariffs that Canada plans to impose on 8 September. In Portland, Oregon, Mike Roach and Kim Osgood, owners of Paloma Clothing say the price of one of their best-selling items - specially designed pillows made in Canada - could shoot up by around 50% to $90. For now, they are holding out on keeping the prices steady, hoping that the "tariff problem" is worked out soon, said Roach. "It would be one thing if we had three months' notice - that would be something you could plan around, do some work with the vendors," he said. "But when it happens literally overnight you're really stuck." The rapidly escalating trade war is also raising questions about the other country in North America - Mexico - and the trade pact between the three neighbours known as the USMCA. Both Canada and Mexico have said they want the USMCA extended for another 16 years, but the US has said it will not renew in its current form. The pact underpins $1.6tn in North American Trade. Escalating trade tensions mean "the risk of the USMCA unravelling has increased", experts from the Oxford Economics forecasting firm warned on Monday. That, in turn, "would plunge Canada into recession and leave it on a permanently lower growth path". Additional reporting by Ana Faguy. Related topics - Published20 hours ago - Published2 days ago

item.title: King of Norway's health has worsened, palace says
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c36lnekj659o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
King of Norway's health has worsened, palace says - Published King Harald V of Norway's health has worsened, the palace has said, as he remains in hospital receiving antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his bloodstream. The monarch has responded to treatment despite the deterioration in his condition, according to the palace, but he will remain at Oslo University Hospital, Rikshospitalet, and on leave from royal duties until further notice. The 89-year-old, who has been on the throne since 1991, was admitted to hospital and put on sick leave a week ago. His son, Crown Prince Haakon, 53, has been serving as regent while his father is on leave. King Harald has been treated in recent weeks with cortisone for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia. It causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced, and leads to fatigue and shortness of breath. In April 2024, Norway's royal household said that King Harald would make a "permanent reduction" to his public engagements "out of consideration for his age". That year, the king had been fitted with a pacemaker after falling ill on holiday in Malaysia. The Norwegian royal family has already faced a challenging year in 2026. Crown Prince Haakon's wife, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, received a lung transplant in June after she had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis in 2018. The transplant came two days after Mette-Marit's son Marius Borg Høiby was sentenced to four years in prison after being convicted of two counts of rape. He had denied the most serious charges and his lawyers said he would appeal the sentence. Høiby, 29, was four when his mother married Crown Prince Haakon and is not himself a royal figure. Also earlier in the year, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. She later apologised to Norway's king and queen for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him. item.title: Israel warns of 'forceful' response to kites flown from Gaza
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y58g2dp3xo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Israel warns of 'forceful' response to kites flown from Gaza - Published Israel has warned Hamas that it will increase strikes on Gaza following concern over launches of kites, drones and balloons from the territory. Several kites were found in an Israeli community near the border with Gaza over the weekend, local media reported. "Forceful actions will be taken to put an end to this phenomenon," Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Monday. Before the war, kites and balloons carrying incendiary devices were launched into Israel, causing fires that burned forest and farmland. Hamas has denied responsibility for the new kites - which were not carrying explosives - and said they belonged to "children searching for their innocent childhood amid the rubble". The group also accused Israel of using the kites as a "pretext" for continued air strikes in Gaza despite the ceasefire agreed last October. - Families' agonising search for answers as thousands still missing in Gaza - Published6 days ago Four kites were found in Kibbutz Nahal Oz, which is about 800m (2,620ft) from the Gaza border, on Friday and Saturday. Several more were found elsewhere in southern Israel last week, according to local media. The Israeli reports cited military sources as saying they believed Hamas was behind the kites and that they might have been intended to test Israel's response. No suspicious materials were attached to the kites and they did not pose a threat, the military said. But Katz warned there would be "zero tolerance" and said: "A balloon is treated like a kite, and a kite is treated like a drone, with or without explosives." Residents of Nahal Oz said in a statement that they feared the return of incendiary kites and balloons, adding: "We will not accept a policy of containment when it comes to our security." Hamas warned of "the danger of the allegations and threats" from Israel and said the kites were "basically children's toys from displacement camps". "These threats are based on fabricated pretexts and are an attempt to justify the continuation of the aggression and violations against our people," a spokesman for the group added. On Sunday, Palestinian health officials said two people were killed and seven others injured in two Israeli strikes in Nuseirat refugee camp and the town of al-Zawayda, both in central Gaza. A four-year-old boy called Mohammed Taha was killed when a building in al-Zawayda, just north of Maghazi refugee camp, was bombed, according to local media. The Israeli military said it killed the commander of a Hamas weapons manufacturing site in the Maghazi area, whom it identified as Ismail Abu Ful, and that it had warned the residents to evacuate beforehand. "There is no ceasefire, there is nothing," Abu Ahmed, a displaced man who had been sheltering nearby, told Reuters news agency. "We want solutions, we want to live in peace." On Monday, Palestinian media reported that a man called Mohammed Abu Asad was killed in an overnight Israeli strike on a tent in the central town of Deir al-Balah. The Israeli military said Abu Asad was a member of the elite Nukhba forces of Hamas's military wing who had taken part in the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on southern Israel. The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to the cross-border assault, during which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage. More than 74,420 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since then, including 1,288 since the ceasefire took effect, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry.

item.title: Russia's second-biggest online retailer targeted in Ukrainian strikes
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg598yvrzpro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Russia's second-biggest online retailer targeted in Ukrainian strikes - Published Warehouses belonging to Russia's second-largest online retailer have been hit by a wave of Ukrainian drone strikes. Ozon said its logistics facilities in the southern regions of Krasnodar, Dagestan, Stavropol and Adygea were on fire and several people had been injured following overnight strikes. Ukraine has for weeks struck sites belonging to Wildberries, the country's biggest online retailer, describing the firm as a legitimate target because it supplied components to the military, which Moscow denies. Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Saturday that Ukraine had opened "Pandora's box" by striking economic targets and that Russia would hit back at Kyiv's "most sensitive economic sectors". Russia has targeted Ukraine's civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022, and recent Russian attacks have hit Ukrainian warehouses and cargo terminals. Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians. Ozon said "a fire broke out" at a logistics centre in Makhachkala, in the southern region of Dagestan, following a drone attack at around 05:00 local time (02:00 GMT) on Monday. The company said earlier that a "major fire" was burning at one of its logistics centres in the city of Krasnodar, 700km (435 miles) to the east of the Dagestan site. Russia's defence ministry said three children had been killed in Krasnodar following a Ukrainian drone attack. Russia's children's rights commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova said they were aged 13, 15 and 16, while six more children had been taken to hospital. Meanwhile, Ozon workers in Adygeysk, in the Adygea region, and Nevinnomyssk, in the Stavropol region, have been evacuated. Videos posted on social media of the Ozon attacks have been verified by the BBC. One shows a drone hitting a warehouse in the Orenburg region, while another shows a large plume of smoke and flames rising from its warehouse in Dagestan. Shares in Ozon fell by as much as 12% on the Moscow Exchange on Monday morning, while shares in its major shareholder, private equity firm AFK Sistema, fell by almost 13%. When asked on Monday whether the Russian government would provide state support to Ozon, the Kremlin said it was "working with business representatives to develop various options for providing support in this difficult situation". The overnight strikes comes a day after Ozon's site in the Samara region was hit. The company said a number of its workers had been injured. Following that strike, Ukraine's defence ministry said on Saturday: "Systematic strikes on dual-use goods storage centres complicate the enemy's logistics and negatively affect the Russian economy as a whole. "After Ukrainian units hit 15 of the largest logistics hubs of Wildberries, it was Ozon's turn." Meanwhile, in Ukraine's Odesa region, overnight strikes targeted food storage facilities and energy infrastructure leading to five people being injured, the region's head Oleg Kiper said on Telegram. Founded in 1998, Ozon is one of Russia's first online retailers. The company is second only to Wildberries in terms of scale and presence, with its pick-up posts and delivery boxes stationed across the country. Both the Ozon and Wildberries logos are often seen together in Russia at shared pick-up points. The targeting of these online retailers has had the effect of bringing the war closer to ordinary Russians. Both companies have been described as "Russia's Amazon" and it is estimated that they are used by 85-90% of Russia's economically active population. In many remote places lacking accessible shops, Russians depend on them for much of their clothes and household appliances. But unlike Amazon, which sells goods directly alongside its marketplace business, Wildberries and Ozon act almost entirely as marketplaces, connecting independent sellers with buyers across Russia, storing and delivering their goods and handling payments. This means many of the losses incurred in the attacks have been borne by those businesses. The Kremlin has denied that online platforms are used for army supplies.

item.title: NZ religious sect leader jailed over death of Chinese follower
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3d79z4z953o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
NZ religious sect leader jailed over death of Chinese follower - Published A New Zealand court has jailed a religious sect leader over the death of an elderly follower who had travelled from China to live with his family. Kaixiao Liu was found guilty of manslaughter and kidnapping, and sentenced to more than 10 years in prison. The body of 70-year-old Shulai Wang had been found wrapped in rice bags near Auckland's Gulf Harbour in March 2024, sparking a major homicide investigation which eventually led to Liu. Liu, a musician who previously appeared in a talent show in China, had denied the charges. He also denied he is a cult leader and said he only attracted followers through his music. During the trial the court heard that Wang had travelled from Hainan island in China to New Zealand in August 2023. She moved in with Liu and his family at their house, which Liu had called "the Ark", along with several other female followers. Prosecutors said that the women acted in "servitude" to Liu and his family, and their lives were tightly controlled by Liu, where they referred to him as "Lord" or "Master". Wang reportedly spent her days taking care of Liu's children, studying scripture, and planting vegetables. The court heard that Wang had struggled to comply with the strict rules, possibly due to her old age, and was frequently disciplined. In March 2024, Wang tried to escape but was caught and restrained. She died later that day, the court heard. The court heard that Liu, his family, and his followers dumped Wang's body near a marina at Gulf Harbour. Liu had taken his children along for the trip "as camouflage". The body was found by a fisherman days later. Police eventually traced the rice bags used to wrap Wang's body to Liu, who had made unusually large purchases of that brand of rice. Besides Liu, his wife, Lanyue Xiao, was sentenced to nearly eight years in jail for kidnapping and manslaughter, amongst other charges. His mother, Xiuyun Li and father, Jingui Liu, had earlier been convicted of kidnapping and misconduct to human remains and are due to be sentenced later this year. On Tuesday's sentencing, Liu's lawyer asked for leniency arguing that his client feels remorse and "is not a cult leader, nor requires people to follow his cult", according to Radio New Zealand. New Zealand media outlets reported that Liu had attended a military-based university in China. In 2011, he was a contestant for China's Got Talent - clips posted online showed him singing onstage blindfolded. Sometime in 2017, he moved to New Zealand along with Xiao, and the couple became permanent residents. Liu attracted followers on Chinese social media where he posted religious discussions, video diaries, and clips of himself singing. He also set up a project called Universal Choir that produced cosmic-themed orchestral music. During the trial a police officer who interviewed one of Liu's female followers gave testimony. He said in court that the woman told him she "met the people over the internet through a song website, and she referred to the occupants of the house as friends". During the sentencing, Justice Mathew Downs said Liu had shown "callous indifference" towards Wang. "Because of you, Ms Wang died a lonely, frightening death. You display no remorse whatsoever. You should feel shame."

item.title: Songs created by AI banned from Australia's music charts
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c20vl4vm2pno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Songs created by AI banned from Australia's music charts - Published Songs that are largely or wholly created by AI have been banned from Australia's music charts. From this week, all releases must be "substantially human made" to be eligible. The Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) said the new code would help "promote the human nature of artistry". It follows a controversy around a cover of Madonna's Like A Prayer by Australian DJ Josh Fawaz which recently topped the ARIA dance singles chart and peaked at number 2 on the country's overall chart. The song has become a staple of commercial radio station playlists and been streamed more than 48 million times on Spotify alone. Fawaz later added generative AI credits to the song after a backlash. ARIA said that Australian artists were competing for attention "in the most crowded market in history" and that it was "not interested in promoting or celebrating the success of AI-generated music that does not contain human artistry". Under the new rules, AI assistance can still be used, but humans must have written the song, and have performed the lead vocal and primary instruments. AI can also still be used for mastering songs and, for example, using drum machines and auto tune. Earlier this year a song was banned from Sweden's music charts because it was created by AI. And in July, the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) said AI guidelines would be rolled out in Latin America, the Middle East, Africa and Southeast Asia for use in their official charts. The updated code, based on the IFPI directive, also excludes music that raises "stream or chart manipulation concerns". ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said: "These changes reflect our intent to remain dynamic and promote the human nature of artistry in what is, to say the least, a rapidly developing space." "Artists already use AI tools in their work, the charts can and should evolve to keep room for that, but music generated wholesale by services built on artists' recordings is a different matter." She added: "A chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent." Artists will be required to declare AI use when they submit a song for chart consideration. ARIA said that if it later emerged music was largely AI-generated it could retrospectively adjust chart positions, and if the piece topped the charts, it may request that awards given for reaching Number One were returned. Artists and their representatives will be able to challenge their exclusion. Among the artists supporting the move are Australian electronic act Peking Duk. Last month, they shared an AI-assisted version of their 2014 hit High on Instagram, captioned: "When you re-record your own song with AI so Australian radio will play it." Band member Adam Hyde told Channel Nine's Today show that AI-generated music was "removing the human experience from life". In July this year, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese promised "the strongest possible protection" from AI for Australian creatives. Albanese pledged that writers and musicians would be able to choose if and how their work was used in the training of AI, saying it would be "theft" if creatives lost that control and were not paid for its use. item.title: Outrage in Nepal over rape and murder of three-year-old girl
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgy58ql288o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Outrage in Nepal over rape and murder of three-year-old girl - Published Activists and politicians in Nepal have urged the government to enact tougher laws as the alleged rape and murder of a three-year-old girl has caused outrage across the country. Nepal has seen continued protests since the girl was found dead last week, three days after she went missing in Madhesh province. Nine people have been arrested in connection with the case, a local police spokesman told the BBC. The crime has triggered demands for reform. Police have also been accused of negligence in the initial stages of the investigation after footage of a teenage suspect was leaked onto social media. After days of demonstrations in the city of Simara, the victim's family met government ministers, and secured a written agreement over the weekend. The government has promised to review laws on serious offences, and create a memorial in honour of the child. The incident has also opened a wider debate over how Nepal deals with young offenders, with some campaigners pushing for harsher punishments for minors convicted of rape or murder. Prominent human rights activist Gauri Pradhan called the attack a "very painful incident and the government should punish anyone involved in such atrocious act. There should be some serious efforts for wider reforms". However, he cautioned against calls for the introduction of the death penalty. There has also been anger after a video showing a teenage suspect giving a statement about the suspected murder was uploaded to social media, sparking questions as to how footage of the individual under police custody was leaked. "We have so far found one police personnel directly involved in the [leak] and have initiated action against him," chief district officer of Bara district, Dharmendra Kumar Mishra, told the BBC. "If more officers are found, they will also be punished. We have zero tolerance against such practice." More than 25,500 accusations of rape and sexual abuse were filed between July 2017 to July 2025, according to Nepalese Police. Of these cases, more than 3,200 female victims were under the age of 10, the police say.

item.title: Sonya Massey's killer Sean Grayson dies in US prison
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgrvj28wrxgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Sonya Massey's killer Sean Grayson dies in US prison - Published Sean Grayson, the white US police officer convicted of murdering a black woman, Sonya Massey, during an incident at her home in 2024, has died in prison at age 32. Grayson shot dead Massey, 36, during an exchange that took place after she reported a suspected intruder at her residence in Illinois. The killing reignited the debate about police brutality in the US. Grayson said he fired because he thought Massey was about to throw a pot of boiling water on him. He was last year found guilty of second-degree murder. The former police officer was undergoing treatment for colon cancer. His lawyer Daniel Fultz confirmed to the BBC that Grayson had died on Sunday, but did not disclose the cause. The BBC has asked the Illinois Department of Corrections for comment. Lawyers for Massey's family said: "Grayson's death in custody from cancer does not bring Sonya back." "We wish his family prayers of peace, as we do for all who grieve a loved one. Sonya's family knows that pain all too well and will grieve her loss the rest of their days," the lawyers said, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner. Protests took place across the US in the aftermath of Massey's death, and then-President Joe Biden declared that the late woman "should be alive today". - Ex-officer guilty of murder of Sonya Massey after she reported suspected intruder - Published29 October 2025 The incident took place in the early hours over Independence Day weekend in July 2024. Massey called police to her home in Springfield, 200 miles (320km) south of Chicago, to report that she believed someone had broken in to her property. Police bodycam footage of the incident showed the chaotic sequence of events. The shooting happened after an exchange of words about a pot on Massey's stove. Massey and Grayson appeared to laugh over her pot of "steaming hot water", before Massey twice said: "I rebuke you in the name of Jesus." "You better [expletive] not or I swear to God I'll [expletive] shoot you in your [expletive] face," Grayson said. He then drew his pistol as he shouted for her to drop the pot. "OK, I'm sorry," Massey was heard saying before she ducked. Grayson fired three shots, striking her in the face. Grayson, who was subsequently sacked from his job, was charged with first-degree murder, but the jury was allowed to convict him of the lesser charge of second-degree murder. He was sentenced to 20 years in prison. In recent months, he applied for release on medical grounds, but was unsuccessful. He had been diagnosed with cancer in 2023.

item.title: Access to Zambian courts prevented as election petition deadline looms
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgrvjn88rxqo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Zambia courts sealed off as election petition deadline looms - Published Court premises in the Zambian capital, Lusaka, and elsewhere have been shut as the deadline for filing a petition against the outcome of the recent presidential election approaches. An unusual police presence has been reported at some courts, which have been taped off to prevent access. Opposition candidate Brian Mundubile said he would challenge the election result, citing irregularities, after coming second with a 38% share of the vote. Incumbent Hakainde Hichilema won a second term with 60%. Mundubile is in hiding over alleged threats made against him, amid a post-election period marked by controversy, including the shooting dead of an opposition figure and the arrest of others. Monday is the last day on which petition against the presidential election result can be filed. Such a petition could potentially affect the inauguration of Hichilema, which is scheduled for 1 September. On Monday, lawyers who arrived at the courts were being asked to depart. One lawyer told the BBC that three armed men approached his vehicle, identified themselves, and instructed him to leave the area. The courts that have been sealed off include the High Court in Lusaka, the Supreme Court, which also houses the Constitutional Court, and several local courts. It is unclear when the premises will reopen. The BBC has contacted the Zambian police and the judiciary for comment. Local media cite a directive by a judiciary administrative official telling all staff not to report to work following the closure of courts for "security reasons". The memo, which has also been shared online by some opposition figures, does not give details of the security situation. Some commentators have raised concerns over the closure while questioning the independence of the judiciary. A prominent voice for the opposition, Emmanuel Mwamba, alleged the action was aimed at preventing Mundubile from filing his presidential election petition. The Law Association of Zambia (LAZ) said it was concerned by the closure of the courts and the presence of heavily armed military personnel around court premises in Lusaka. It said there was no formal public explanation for the closure nor its expected duration. Referring to the "unsigned memorandum" from the judiciary addressing staff, it said no further official information had been provided to lawyers and the public. "The closure of the courts has immediate implications for access to justice, particularly for persons requiring urgent judicial intervention," it said in a statement It said the timing was "particularly significant in the present electoral context", citing a "seven-day period" in which a person may "petition the Constitutional Court to nullify the election of a President-elect". Despite the court closure, preparations for Hichilema's inauguration appear to be continuing. The youth and sport ministry has issued a media invitation for journalists to accompany a cabinet official on an inspection of arrangements at National Heroes Stadium, where the ceremony is expected to take place. Mundubile last week rejected the presidential election results and said he planned to challenge the outcome through the courts. He remains in a secure location under the protection of what his campaign describes as an "international human rights body". He went into hiding after the arrests of opposition figures and the death of former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya during a raid by security officers, in what officials described as an exchange of fire in a security operation in the capital. The arrests as well as the death of Kafwaya prompted calls from rights groups and the Law Association of Zambia for an independent investigations. Amnesty International described the Kafwaya's killing as "deeply alarming" and called for prompt, thorough and impartial investigations. The lawyers' association similarly expressed "grave concern" and demanded investigation. The election day, 13 August, was described by regional and international observers as largely peaceful, but they raised concerns about late electoral reforms, media freedom and access to the media in the run-up to the poll. The EU observation mission said restrictions on the opposition may have contributed to an "uneven contest". On vote tallying, the mission described a heavy military presence as intimidating and said it had received reports of attacks on some tallying centres. It said staff in many centres did not record results on tally sheets as soon as they were announced, and cited weak verification between digital entries and paper records. It added that returning officers frequently paused proceedings while awaiting instructions from headquarters. The EU mission also called for "maximal transparency" over the poll outcome, noting that the electoral commission did not publish separate polling-station results You may also be interested in: - Ex-Zambian minister killed in security raid on opposition - Published4 days ago - Top Zambian opposition figures arrested days after presidential vote - Published17 August Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent.
